Pantoliano has met with representatives of both the Obama and McCain campaigns to promote mental health and recovery. The founder and president of No Kidding, Me Too, an eight-month-old advocacy organization, Pantoliano also released a teaser for his new film about various forms of mental illness.

At the CNN Grill, he answered five questions for CNN.com.

**CNN.com: What are you doing here in Denver?**

**Pantoliano:** I’ve always been fascinated by the political process, ever since I was a kid. ... I’ve always loved the festive atmosphere, the camaraderie and working for a candidate—whether it was someone in the 3rd Ward, where I lived in Hoboken, New Jersey, or a senator, a congressman or even a president. I remember when President Kennedy came to Hoboken in 1961; I was only 10 years old. I was with the Kennedys tonight.

**CNN.com: Are you a Barack Obama supporter?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m advocating for my organization. I’m going to the Republican National Convention next week. I’m speaking about mental illness and the miracles of recovery; that’s what the movie is about. I’ve met with Obama’s chief of staff and other members of his team, and I’ve met with McCain’s people. Mental illness is at the forefront of their minds.

**CNN.com: Who are you voting for?**

**Pantoliano:** I don’t know yet.

*Watch how celebrity endorsements can backfire »*

**CNN.com: Where are the hot spots in Denver? Where are people gathering?**

**Pantoliano:** Here, at the CNN Grill. It’s all they’re talking about. I really like Denver. The security is less kinetic than it was four years ago. That whole climate of fear that this administration has played on our nerves—I think I have post-traumatic stress from it. What happened was that I became addicted to the news.

*iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share the sights and sounds.*

**CNN.com: Do you think attending a convention helps you make up your mind more effectively than sitting in your living room?**

**Pantoliano:** I’m an independent. I can be inspired tonight by Michelle Obama’s speech, and then something may happen next week, so I go back and forth. I’m a flip-flopper. The difference I see between Republicans and Democrats is that the Democrats truly reflect the melting pot of our society. Obama really represents that. Obama represents what America is today.

CNN’s Michael Senzon contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Joe Pantoliano, the actor and filmmaker best known for portraying Ralph Cifaretto on HBO’s “The Sopranos,” was at the Democratic National Convention on Monday to draw attention to the experiences of people with mental illness.

Pantoliano has spoken with representatives from both Barack Obama’s and John McCain’s campaigns about mental health and recovery. He is the founder and president of No Kidding, Me Too, an advocacy group established eight months ago. He also unveiled a preview of his upcoming film examining several types of mental illness.

During a visit to the CNN Grill, Pantoliano responded to five questions from CNN.com.

**CNN.com: Why have you come to Denver?**

**Pantoliano:** Politics has intrigued me since childhood. I have always enjoyed the celebrations, sense of fellowship and work involved in supporting a candidate—whether that person was running in Hoboken’s 3rd Ward, where I lived in New Jersey, or seeking office as a member of Congress, a senator or president. I still remember President Kennedy visiting Hoboken in 1961, when I was just 10. Tonight, I spent time with members of the Kennedy family.

**CNN.com: Do you support Barack Obama?**

**Pantoliano:** My purpose is to represent my organization. Next week, I will also attend the Republican National Convention. I am talking about mental illness and the remarkable possibility of recovery, which is the subject of the film. I have met with Obama’s chief of staff and other members of his team, as well as people from McCain’s campaign. Mental illness is an issue they are actively considering.

**CNN.com: Which candidate will receive your vote?**

**Pantoliano:** I have not decided.

*See how endorsements from celebrities can have unintended consequences.*

**CNN.com: What are Denver’s popular gathering places? Where is everyone spending time?**

**Pantoliano:** The CNN Grill is the place everyone is discussing. I like Denver a lot. Security feels less intense than it did four years ago. This administration has repeatedly used fear to affect people’s emotions, and I think it has left me with something like post-traumatic stress. I ended up becoming hooked on following the news.

*iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share what you are seeing and hearing.*

**CNN.com: Does attending a political convention help you reach a decision more effectively than watching from home?**

**Pantoliano:** I am an independent voter. Michelle Obama’s speech might motivate me tonight, but something could occur next week that changes my thinking. I keep moving between the two sides—I am a flip-flopper. One distinction I notice is that the Democratic Party more closely reflects the cultural melting pot that makes up American society. Obama embodies that diversity and represents the America of today.

CNN’s Michael Senzon contributed to the report.

# Joe Pantoliano brings mental health campaign to Democratic convention

**DENVER, Colorado** — Actor Joe Pantoliano came to the Democratic National Convention with a message extending beyond politics: Mental illness should be discussed without shame.

Pantoliano, known for roles in “The Sopranos,” “The Matrix” and “Memento,” attended the Denver convention to promote **No Kidding, Me Too!**, the nonprofit organization he founded to challenge the stigma surrounding mental illness.

The Emmy-winning actor has spoken publicly about his own experience with clinical depression and has encouraged others in the entertainment industry to share their stories. His campaign argues that candid conversations can help people recognize symptoms and seek treatment.

Amid the convention’s speeches, delegates and celebrity appearances, Pantoliano said he wanted mental health to be treated as a mainstream health-care issue rather than a private failing. His visit also highlighted the role public figures can play in changing how depression, addiction and other conditions are portrayed.

Below is a five-question interview with Pantoliano, with his responses paraphrased for clarity.

### CNN: Why bring a mental health campaign to a political convention?

**Pantoliano:** Decisions made by political leaders affect access to diagnosis, treatment and insurance coverage. A national convention offers an opportunity to put mental health before policymakers, activists and the media at the same time.

### CNN: Why did you decide to discuss your own depression publicly?

**Pantoliano:** For years, he did not fully understand what he was experiencing. Receiving a diagnosis helped him see depression as a medical condition, not a character flaw. Speaking openly, he said, can make it easier for others to ask for help.

### CNN: What does “No Kidding, Me Too!” mean?

**Pantoliano:** The phrase is intended to create solidarity. When one person reveals that he or she lives with mental illness, others often recognize that they—or someone close to them—have had a similar experience. That shared recognition can reduce isolation and shame.

### CNN: Can Hollywood help change public attitudes?

**Pantoliano:** Entertainment can either reinforce stereotypes or present people with mental illness as complex human beings. Actors, writers and producers have the ability to tell more accurate stories, while celebrities can use their visibility to normalize conversations about treatment and recovery.

### CNN: What do you want convention attendees to take away?

**Pantoliano:** Mental health should be considered part of overall health. People should not be embarrassed to seek professional help, and public policy should make effective care easier to obtain.

Pantoliano’s appearance added a personal issue to a convention dominated by campaign strategy and policy debate. His central argument was straightforward: The more people talk honestly about mental illness, the harder it becomes to treat those living with it as outsiders.

**Q&A: Joe Pantoliano brings a bipartisan mental-health message to Denver**

**DENVER —** Actor Joe Pantoliano, known for roles in *The Sopranos*, *The Matrix* and *Memento*, stopped by the CNN Grill during the Democratic National Convention to discuss his campaign to end the stigma surrounding mental illness. The following is an edited Q&A.

**Q: What brings you to the Democratic convention?**  
**Pantoliano:** I’m here to talk about mental health and the stigma that keeps people from seeking help. After dealing with my own clinical depression, I started the nonprofit No Kidding, Me Too! The goal is to make it acceptable for people to say they have a mental illness—and to show that recovery is possible.

**Q: Are you here on behalf of the Democratic Party?**  
**Pantoliano:** No. I’m not here as a party spokesman or to campaign for a candidate. Personally, I’m an independent. I look at the issues and the people rather than automatically following one party.

**Q: Where do you stand politically?**  
**Pantoliano:** I have views that cross party lines. There are things I agree with Democrats about and things I agree with Republicans about. But mental illness isn’t Democratic or Republican. It affects every kind of family, regardless of income, religion or political affiliation.

**Q: You also plan to attend the Republican National Convention. Why?**  
**Pantoliano:** For exactly that reason. If we want better treatment, insurance coverage and public understanding, we have to talk to both sides. I’m bringing the same message to the Republican convention that I’m bringing here: People should not be ashamed to ask for help, and mental-health care should be treated as health care.

**Q: What do you want conventiongoers to take away from your visit?**  
**Pantoliano:** That silence can be dangerous. The more people speak openly about depression and other illnesses, the easier it becomes for someone who is struggling to reach out. This issue is bigger than party politics.

# Joe Pantoliano turns the spotlight on mental illness recovery

**DENVER** — Joe Pantoliano has made a career playing men who command attention, from the treacherous Ralph Cifaretto on “The Sopranos” to memorable roles in “The Matrix,” “Memento” and “Risky Business.” Away from the screen, however, the actor is focused on a subject Hollywood often keeps in the shadows: mental illness.

Pantoliano, who has spoken publicly about his experience with depression, says recovery begins by replacing shame with honest conversation. Through his nonprofit, No Kidding, Me Too!, he has encouraged people living with mental illness — along with their families — to speak openly and seek help.

His latest project extends that mission to film. Pantoliano is sharing a teaser for a documentary centered on mental health, recovery and the effect psychiatric illness can have on entire families. Rather than presenting recovery as a simple Hollywood transformation, the project emphasizes that it can be an uneven, continuing process supported by treatment, community and candor.

The actor hopes the documentary will help challenge the stigma that keeps many people from asking for help. For Pantoliano, telling personal stories is not about seeking sympathy; it is about showing viewers that mental illness is common, treatable and not a moral failing.

## Politics, conventions and Obama

Pantoliano brought that message to Denver amid the energy of the Democratic National Convention, where politics, entertainment and advocacy converged.

He expressed enthusiasm about Barack Obama’s ability to inspire voters and broaden participation in the political process. But Pantoliano was also careful not to describe himself as a loyal member of either major party.

He identifies as an independent voter, he said, and prefers to judge candidates individually rather than follow a party label. That independence allows him to admire Obama while maintaining the right to question any candidate’s positions — particularly on health care, veterans’ services and mental-health policy.

Political conventions, Pantoliano suggested, can offer more than speeches and carefully staged television moments. They also give advocates an opportunity to put overlooked issues before lawmakers, delegates and the public.

## Finding Denver beyond the convention floor

When the schedule allows, Denver offers plenty of escapes from convention crowds. Lower Downtown, better known as LoDo, combines restaurants, galleries and historic brick buildings near Union Station. The pedestrian-friendly 16th Street area provides a quick introduction to the center of the city, while Larimer Square is a popular stop for dining and nightlife.

For visitors with more time, Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre offers a dramatic look at Colorado’s landscape just outside the city. Denver’s arts district, museums and independent restaurants provide quieter alternatives to the political events filling downtown hotels and meeting halls.

Still, Pantoliano’s central destination is wherever he can find an audience willing to talk about mental health.

After years of playing characters who hide their vulnerabilities, he is now using his public profile to argue that acknowledging them can be an act of strength. His documentary teaser is only a glimpse of that effort, but the message is already clear: Recovery should not have to happen in silence.
